  collapse = TRUE,

```{r load-package}
library(mixeff)
```

`fit_status()` reports the convergence status of a model fitted by
`lmm()` or `glmm()`. This vignette explains interior and reduced-rank
solutions, the test for singularity, and the use of `verify_convergence()`
to check a fitted optimum. It also describes what happens when the
engine substitutes a different GLMM estimator.

## Interior solutions

The first example is a small longitudinal study with twelve clinics,
a week effect, and a treatment contrast.

```{r clinic-data, include = FALSE}
set.seed(42)
n_clinic <- 12L
n_per_clinic <- 6L
clinic <- factor(rep(seq_len(n_clinic), each = n_per_clinic))
week <- rep(0:(n_per_clinic - 1L), n_clinic)
treatment <- factor(
  rep(rep(c("usual", "coached"), each = n_per_clinic), length.out = length(week)),
  levels = c("usual", "coached")
)
clinic_shift <- rnorm(n_clinic, sd = 0.45)
score <- 7.2 - 0.28 * week - 0.55 * (treatment == "coached") +
  clinic_shift[as.integer(clinic)] + rnorm(length(week), sd = 0.35)
clinic_visits <- data.frame(score, week, treatment, clinic)
```

```{r interior-fit}
fit <- lmm(
  score ~ week + treatment + (1 | clinic),
  clinic_visits,
  control = mm_control(verbose = -1)
)
fit_status(fit)
```

`converged_interior` means the engine accepted a finite interior
solution under its convergence rules, with every variance component
away from zero. Individual derivative checks can still be unavailable;
the certificate below records which checks completed. The status does
not establish global optimality, correct model specification, or that
the data carry enough information.

Three statuses distinguish the main outcomes:

- `converged_interior` — the engine accepted a finite interior solution
  under its convergence rules.
- `converged_reduced_rank` — the engine accepted a solution whose
  random-effect covariance has lower rank than requested.
- `not_optimized` — the run stopped without certifying a stationary
  point, for example in a flat or boundary region. Estimates are present,
  but convergence has not been established. `summary()` also records
  this status in a `Notes:` line.

Optimization is silent and runs within one native call under bounded
evaluation budgets; the `lmm()`/`glmm()` help pages and `?mm_control`
document the budgets and how to cap them.

`optimizer_certificate()` reports the optimizer, stopping condition,
and checks used to assign the convergence status:

```{r interior-certificate}
optimizer_certificate(fit)
```

For joint-Laplace GLMMs, optimizer evidence and inference covariance are
separate records. The fit-time optimizer certificate does not include a full
Hessian assessment over fixed effects (beta) and covariance parameters (theta);
it labels that check `not_assessed`, with the stage in the reason. Optimization
may still compute a Hessian for polishing. The label does not mean that a
Hessian computation failed.

The later inference stage attempts a central finite-difference Hessian of
minus twice the log likelihood over beta and interior theta coordinates.
It omits theta coordinates too close to their lower bounds for central
differences. When this Hessian passes its checks, fixed-effect covariance
is twice the beta block of its inverse. If that route fails, an available
RX fallback conditions on theta and carries a different method and lower
reliability. Inspect `attr(vcov(gfit), "mm_method")`, `"mm_status"`,
`"mm_reliability"`, and `"mm_notes"` for the actual route and its scope.
A successful inference calculation does not rewrite the fit-time certificate.

Raw gradient norms depend on parameter coordinates and are not measures of
coefficient precision. Curvature-scaled stationarity evidence, when available,
is recorded separately in `optimizer_certificate(gfit)$raw$stationarity_decrement`.
Read both with their stated tolerances; a small scaled quantity does not change
the qualification recorded in an approximate raw-gradient certificate.

```{r interior-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(inherits(fit, "mm_lmm"))
stopifnot(identical(fit_status(fit), "converged_interior"))
stopifnot(isFALSE(is_singular(fit)))
stopifnot(nrow(optimizer_certificate(fit)$table) > 0L)
```

## Boundary and reduced-rank fits

The next example produces a singular fit. We simulate ten daily
reaction-time measurements for each of eighteen subjects, with nearly
perfectly correlated subject intercepts and slopes.

```{r singular-data, include = FALSE}
set.seed(3)
n_subj <- 18L
days <- 0:9
b0 <- rnorm(n_subj, sd = 30)
b1 <- 0.5 * b0 / 30 * 10 + rnorm(n_subj, sd = 0.5)

sleep_like <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_subj), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    subj = factor(i),
    days = days,
    rt = 250 + b0[i] + (10 + b1[i]) * days +
      rnorm(length(days), sd = 20)
  )
}))
```

`lme4::lmer()` reports `boundary (singular) fit` for this model:

```{r lme4-side, eval = requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)}
m <- suppressMessages(lme4::lmer(
  rt ~ days + (1 + days | subj),
  data = sleep_like
))
m
lme4::isSingular(m)
```

In `mixeff`, `fit_status()` reports the convergence outcome and
`is_singular()` tests for singularity. For more detail, `diagnostics()`
returns codes with severity and stage, while `changes()` compares the
requested model with the effective specification and fitted result.

```{r singular-fit}
sfit <- lmm(
  rt ~ days + (1 + days | subj),
  sleep_like,
  control = mm_control(verbose = -1)
)

fit_status(sfit)
is_singular(sfit)
diagnostics(sfit)$table[, c("code", "severity", "stage", "message")]
changes(sfit)
```

The requested random-effect covariance for `(1 + days | subj)` has two
dimensions: a subject intercept and a subject slope. The fitted covariance
has effective rank one. This is recorded as the `covariance_reduced`
diagnostic and the `converged_reduced_rank` status, which also appears
when the object is printed.

```{r singular-print}
print(sfit)
```

```{r singular-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(fit_status(sfit), "converged_reduced_rank"))
stopifnot(isTRUE(is_singular(sfit)))
diag_codes <- diagnostics(sfit)$table$code
stopifnot("covariance_reduced" %in% diag_codes)
ch <- changes(sfit)$table
stopifnot("design_time_reduction" %in% ch$stage ||
          "covariance_transition" %in% ch$stage)
sfit_print <- capture.output(print(sfit))
stopifnot(any(grepl("reduced_rank|boundary", sfit_print)))
```

A reduced-rank covariance does not automatically invalidate the model,
but it restricts the inference methods available in `mixeff`. These
restrictions are described at the end of this vignette.

## How singularity relates to θ and rank

To read the boundary structure itself, look at the model's internal
coordinates. The random-effect covariance Σ is not optimized directly.
The engine searches over a vector θ that fills a lower-triangular
factor Λ, with Σ = σ²ΛΛᵀ; θ is by construction exactly the set of free
entries of Λ. This is the parameterization Bates et al. (2015)
describe for `lme4`; `MixedModels.jl` and the engine behind `mixeff`
inherit it. `parameterization()` shows the mapping for the singular
fit:

```{r singular-parameterization}
parameterization(sfit)$table[, c("theta_name", "theta_value", "lambda_value")]
```

The *diagonal* entry for the `days` slope is pinned at numerical zero
— that is the boundary event behind the `converged_reduced_rank`
status.

A zero entry in θ does not always imply singularity. A zero
**off-diagonal** entry of Λ can occur in a full-rank covariance. In the
two-dimensional example below, it sets the covariance to zero. In larger
blocks, covariance entries are sums of products, so one zero factor
entry need not make the corresponding covariance zero.

Singularity depends on the rank of the whole covariance matrix. For this
square triangular factor, it occurs exactly when at least one
**diagonal** entry of Λ is zero. The following example contrasts the two
cases:

```{r lambda-rank-demo}
l11 <- 1.2
l21 <- 0.4
l22 <- 0.9

# Zero the OFF-DIAGONAL entry (l21 = 0): zero covariance, full rank.
L_offdiag_zero <- matrix(c(l11, 0, 0, l22), nrow = 2)
Sigma_offdiag_zero <- L_offdiag_zero %*% t(L_offdiag_zero)
Sigma_offdiag_zero
eigen(Sigma_offdiag_zero, symmetric = TRUE)$values

# Zero a DIAGONAL entry (l22 = 0): the rank collapses to 1.
L_diag_zero <- matrix(c(l11, l21, 0, 0), nrow = 2)
Sigma_diag_zero <- L_diag_zero %*% t(L_diag_zero)
Sigma_diag_zero
eigen(Sigma_diag_zero, symmetric = TRUE)$values
```

With the off-diagonal at zero, both eigenvalues are positive: the
intercept and slope are uncorrelated, and each still has its own
variance — a full-rank fit with the covariance structure specified by
`(1 + days || subj)`. With a diagonal entry at zero, one
eigenvalue is zero and the two random effects collapse onto a single
dimension: that is singularity.

```{r lambda-rank-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(qr(Sigma_offdiag_zero)$rank, 2L))
stopifnot(all(eigen(Sigma_offdiag_zero, symmetric = TRUE)$values > 0))
stopifnot(identical(qr(Sigma_diag_zero)$rank, 1L))
ev_diag <- eigen(Sigma_diag_zero, symmetric = TRUE)$values
stopifnot(abs(ev_diag[[2L]]) < 1e-12)
stopifnot(identical(Sigma_offdiag_zero[1L, 2L], 0))
# The fitted singular case: the slope's DIAGONAL theta entry is at zero.
pt <- parameterization(sfit)$table
stopifnot(pt$theta_value[pt$theta_name == "theta[0:days,days]"] < 1e-6)
```

`is_singular()` follows lme4's tolerance rule: it checks whether a
zero-bounded diagonal θ is below `tol` (default `1e-4`). For older fits
without a theta map, it falls back to the recorded engine covariance and
fit statuses. A tolerance-based result can differ from an exact rank verdict.

## Verifying an optimum: `verify_convergence()`

A convergence status describes the run that produced the fit. To check
the stability of that solution, `verify_convergence()` re-runs the fit
under the engine's bounded verification workflow: a restart from the
fitted optimum, one or more jittered restarts, and (LMM-only, opt-in)
an alternate-optimizer consensus pass. The engine judges agreement
against explicit tolerances on the objective, θ, and the fixed
effects, and returns the verdict for R to format.

The R bridge reuses a live fitted handle or restores the saved fitted state
before invoking that workflow. Verification compares its deliberate searches
against the recorded solution, including after reload. If neither a valid
handle nor a compatible snapshot is available, verification refuses rather
than optimizing a replacement baseline.

```{r verify-lmm}
vc <- verify_convergence(fit)
vc
```

The verdict summarizes agreement with the reference optimum within
the printed tolerances
(`restart_agrees`, `optimizer_consensus`, `fragile`, `unstable`, or
`not_run`). A verdict of `restart_agrees` is evidence of a *stable*
optimum — the bounded re-runs came back to the same place — not proof
of a global one. The `consensus` pass defaults to `FALSE` because this
vendored build compiles without the optional `nlopt` backend; for some
models the engine's alternate optimizer choice is an nlopt optimizer,
and its absence would read as a spurious `fragile` verdict that
reflects the build, not the fit.

Verification and rank are different questions. Running the verifier on
the singular fit from above also comes back `restart_agrees`: a
reduced-rank optimum can be stable across restarts.

```{r verify-singular}
vs <- verify_convergence(sfit)
vs$status
```

The GLMM method uses the same workflow with wider default tolerances —
objective `1e-4` and beta `1e-3`, against the LMM defaults of `1e-5`
and `1e-4` — because GLMM objective evaluations include
inner-PIRLS numerical error and the joint path's derivative-free beta search
bounds beta reproducibility at its stopping tolerance. The consensus
pass is refused for GLMM fits (the GLMM fitting routines select their own
optimizers).

```{r glmm-data, include = FALSE}
set.seed(7)
g <- factor(rep(1:12, each = 12))
x <- rnorm(144)
eta <- -0.3 + 0.8 * x + rep(rnorm(12, sd = 0.5), each = 12)
trial <- data.frame(y = rbinom(144, 1, plogis(eta)), x = x, g = g)
```

```{r verify-glmm}
gfit <- glmm(
  y ~ x + (1 | g),
  trial,
  family = binomial(),
  control = mm_control(verbose = -1)
)

gv <- verify_convergence(gfit)
gv
```

```{r verify-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(vc$status, "restart_agrees"))
stopifnot(all(vc$table$agrees))
stopifnot(identical(vc$tolerances$objective, 1e-5))
stopifnot(identical(vc$tolerances$beta, 1e-4))
stopifnot(identical(vs$status, "restart_agrees"))
stopifnot(identical(gv$status, "restart_agrees"))
stopifnot(all(gv$table$agrees))
stopifnot(identical(gv$tolerances$objective, 1e-4))
stopifnot(identical(gv$tolerances$beta, 1e-3))
```

## GLMM estimator substitution

`glmm(method = "joint_laplace")` requests the joint-Laplace estimator,
which supports Wald inference when the fitted covariance passes its
checks. On some designs, the engine cannot certify a joint-Laplace
optimum and returns a fit from the profiled-PIRLS estimator instead.
The substitution is recorded in several places:

- `optimizer_certificate(fit)$raw$estimator_substitution` contains the
  requested and effective methods, the requested method's fit status and
  return code, and the reason for substitution. Use this record in scripts.
- A condition of class `mm_estimator_substitution_notice` reports the
  change when the fit returns. Suppress it with `mm_control(verbose = -1)`.
- `summary()` prints an `estimator substitution:` note naming both
  estimators, regardless of verbosity settings or the fallback fit's
  convergence status.
- `verify_convergence()` restores and checks the effective estimator
  that produced the returned estimates.

When no substitution occurred, the record is absent:

```{r substitution-surface}
optimizer_certificate(gfit)$raw$estimator_substitution
```

```{r substitution-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(is.null(optimizer_certificate(gfit)$raw$estimator_substitution))
```

For example, in a reproduction of a published `glmer()` analysis of OSF
study data, an error-rate model included an open-practice × year
interaction. With raw, uncentered `Year`, the joint-Laplace fit did not
certify and the engine returned a profiled-PIRLS fallback with Wald
inference withheld. Centering the predictor as `Year - 2015` allowed the
joint fit to certify and agree with `glmer()` on the same data.
A scaling advisory identifies the poorly scaled columns; centering or
rescaling them can improve optimization.

## Inference at a boundary

On singular fits, `mixeff` withholds Satterthwaite and Kenward–Roger
degrees of freedom under its validated-support policy. The results
include reason codes, and parametric bootstrap tests remain available.
See `vignette("inference")` for the methods, restrictions, and examples.

## References

- Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B., and Walker, S. (2015). Fitting
  linear mixed-effects models using lme4. *Journal of Statistical
  Software*, 67(1), 1–48. <https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v067.i01>
